question: Does merely factorizing a network into routed modules yield specialization and generalization, or are stronger routing and optimization biases required?

key_findings.claim: The paper builds a controlled factorial benchmark in which the number and identity of ground-truth rules are known, then separates architectural modularity, context-only routing, and oracle routing.
key_findings.evidence: Synthetic MLP, attention, and recurrent generators expose a rule indicator c and use 2, 4, 8, 16, or 32 equiprobable rules. Monolithic, learned Modular, context-only Modular-op, and hard-routed GT-Modular models are compared at roughly matched parameter counts in classification and regression, over five capacities, five sampled tasks, and five seeds, totaling about 20,000 trained models.

key_findings.claim: Perfect rule-to-module routing is consistently valuable as rule count grows, but ordinary end-to-end modular routing remains far from that oracle and increasingly collapses modules.
key_findings.evidence: Across the aggregate performance plots, GT-Modular generally has the lowest error/loss and fastest average convergence. Collapse-Avg, Collapse-Worst, alignment distance, adaptation error, and inverse mutual information all worsen for learned routers as rules increase from 2 to 32; Modular-op improves on learned Modular but remains far from the oracle.

key_findings.claim: The broad conclusion that learned Modular models outperform Monolithic models is architecture- and objective-dependent rather than universal.
key_findings.evidence: The direct head-to-head ranking for RNN regression favors Monolithic in 86.4% of in-distribution tasks and 94.4% of the extreme out-of-distribution tasks; the corresponding performance curves also often place the learned Modular model above the Monolithic loss. By contrast, MLP classification favors Modular 89.6% in-distribution and 83.2% out-of-distribution, and MHA classification favors it 69.6% and 76.4%. The paper's prose does not foreground this reversal.

key_findings.claim: The benchmark cleanly diagnoses routing failure but does not test discovery of latent task structure: every sample supplies the ground-truth rule identity as an input.
key_findings.evidence: All data generators include c, and Modular-op routes only from c while GT-Modular directly clamps routing to c. Thus the gap from Modular-op to GT-Modular is an optimization/specialization gap with privileged context already available, not evidence about recovering unobserved mechanisms from raw real-world data.

key_findings.claim: The function-class inclusion proof does not by itself make the finite, parameter-matched empirical comparison a pure test of inductive bias.
key_findings.evidence: The appendix proves GT-Modular is contained in Modular-op, which is contained in Modular, which is contained in Monolithic only given enough representational capacity and arbitrary functional assignments. Actual experiments roughly equalize total parameters, split that budget differently, restrict each architecture, and optimize by gradient descent; the monolith therefore need not contain a trained modular model at the tested width, and optimization and effective capacity remain confounded.

anchors.section: Appendix B Proof of Model Relations

key_findings.claim: The quantitative scope is large, but the claimed OOD and scaling implications are limited by untuned, noiseless, infinite-data synthetic tasks and mild shifts.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly omit hyperparameter tuning, sample fresh data every iteration, use deterministic linear rules, know the correct module count, and test only input-variance/radius changes and sequence-length extrapolation. They acknowledge that these OOD results are often highly correlated with in-distribution performance and list finite data, noise, latent rule count, compositional shifts, and complex nonlinear rules as future work.

method.core_idea: Treat modular learning as recoverable rule-to-module assignment in synthetic mixtures, and measure utilization, specialization, performance, and extrapolation separately.
method.mechanism: Known rule-conditioned MLP, attention, and recurrent generators create regression and binary-classification targets. Four model classes progressively add routing priors. Performance is accompanied by marginal-load collapse scores, distance from a permutation routing matrix, inverse rule-module mutual information, and a sorted marginal adaptation score.
assumptions: A ground-truth mechanism corresponds one-to-one with exactly one learned module.
Rules are equiprobable for most collapse and specialization metrics and their identity c is observed.
Synthetic linear or nearest-neighbor operations capture the routing difficulty relevant to real modular systems.
Roughly matching parameter counts yields an informative comparison despite different conditional computation and functional allocation.
Variance and sequence-length changes are useful proxies for out-of-distribution generalization.

techniques.role: Generate labeled mixtures with known MLP, attention, or recurrent mechanisms.
Compare no routing prior, learned input routing, context-only routing, and oracle hard routing.
Measure average and worst under-utilization from marginal module activation.
Use Hungarian matching to measure distance from a permutation rule-module assignment.
Measure lack of statistical dependence between rule and selected module.
Compare sorted rule-frequency and module-load marginals across sampled mixtures.

evaluations.setting: About 20,000 MLP, MHA, and RNN models spanning 2-32 rules, five capacities, classification/regression, five tasks, and five seeds.
evaluations.metric: In-distribution and out-of-distribution error/loss plus convergence
evaluations.result: GT-Modular wins most aggregated comparisons and trains fastest; learned Modular is usually much closer to Monolithic than to the oracle.
evaluations.baseline: Monolithic, learned Modular, context-only Modular-op, and oracle GT-Modular.

evaluations.setting: All architectures and objectives aggregated while rule count grows from 2 to 32.
evaluations.metric: Collapse-Avg, Collapse-Worst, alignment, adaptation, and inverse mutual information
evaluations.result: Learned routing collapse and specialization error increase with rule count; Modular-op is better than Modular but substantially worse than GT-Modular.
evaluations.baseline: Uniform random routing has good load balance but poor specialization; GT-Modular is optimal on both.

evaluations.setting: RNN regression, comparing only learned Modular and Monolithic models across tasks and capacities.
evaluations.result: Learned Modular wins only 13.6% in-distribution and 5.6% under the extreme OOD shift.

evaluations.setting: MHA and RNN sequence tasks trained at length 10 and evaluated at lengths 3, 5, 20, and 30, with or without altered token distributions.
evaluations.metric: Classification error or regression L1 loss
evaluations.result: Oracle/context-routed advantages often persist, but trends vary materially by model capacity, task, and architecture.
evaluations.baseline: Matched Monolithic and learned Modular systems.

limitations: Author-stated: no hyperparameter tuning is performed despite heterogeneous model families and optimization behavior.
Author-stated: tasks are deterministic, noiseless, infinite-data, and use simple linear mechanisms; OOD shifts are easy and often track in-distribution performance.
Author-stated: the number of modules is fixed equal to the known number of rules, and most metrics assume equiprobable rules.
Reviewer inference: ground-truth rule context is observed, so the study does not test latent mechanism discovery, imperfect context, or real routing ambiguity.
Reviewer inference: win-count pie charts discard effect size and uncertainty, while the paper reports no paired statistical tests across the many dependent configurations.
Reviewer inference: equal parameter count does not equal equal activated compute, inference cost, or finite-width function class; none of those system costs is reported.
Reviewer inference: the final generalization about learned Modular outperforming Monolithic obscures the opposite result in RNN regression.
failure_modes: A router can balance load perfectly while assigning every rule diffusely, as the random baseline demonstrates.
A router can specialize but map several rules to one expert and leave other experts unused, producing collapse.
Increasing the number of rules makes gradient competition freeze poor assignments and magnifies under-utilization.
Sorted marginal adaptation can look good even when module identity changes across rule distributions, because it does not preserve the rule-module pairing.
Oracle routing gains may disappear when the context label is missing, noisy, or entangled with raw inputs.
A modular parameter split can hurt objectives such as recurrent regression where one shared model exploits capacity more effectively.
reusable_insights: Evaluate modular systems on both utilization and semantic specialization; either metric alone admits trivial failures.
An oracle router is a useful ceiling that separates representation capacity from routing optimization.
Report results by architecture and objective before making aggregate claims, because modularity can reverse direction across regimes.
Benchmarks for modular discovery should hide or corrupt the mechanism label and vary the number of mechanisms independently of module count.
Routing claims need finite-data, compositional-shift, and compute-matched validation in addition to synthetic interpolation.
open_questions: Which regularizer or discrete optimization method closes the oracle routing gap without ground-truth context?
Can specialization be identified when mechanisms overlap, compose, or outnumber the available modules?
How do collapse and specialization behave under noisy, imbalanced, finite-data, and nonstationary rule distributions?
Which metric preserves module identity across distributions while remaining permutation-invariant globally?
Do improvements survive equal activated FLOPs, latency, communication, and hyperparameter tuning on real tasks?

competitive_landscape.title: On The Specialization of Neural Modules
competitive_landscape.difference: Jarvis et al. analyze when linear modules specialize and when specialization is necessary for systematicity, adding learning-dynamics theory and nonlinear validation to this paper's broad empirical diagnosis.

competitive_landscape.title: Improving Expert Specialization in Mixture of Experts
competitive_landscape.difference: Krishnamurthy et al. likewise expose poor decomposition and utilization, then propose an attention-like gate and data-driven regularizer and test them on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-100 rather than stopping at diagnosis.

competitive_landscape.title: Attention for Compositional Modularity
competitive_landscape.difference: Ostapenko et al. test sequential composition of mathematical primitives and similarly find that meaningful routing and privileged structural information drive OOD generalization, extending beyond the one-rule-per-output mixtures here.

competitive_landscape.title: Patch-level Routing in Mixture-of-Experts is Provably Sample-efficient for Convolutional Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This work derives conditional sample-complexity advantages for patch routing and tests matched-parameter WRN mixtures on CelebA/CIFAR, addressing finite-sample and real-image regimes omitted here, though its joint-training theory assumes a proper router.

competitive_landscape.title: Breaking Neural Network Scaling Laws with Modularity
competitive_landscape.difference: Boopathy et al. derive a task-dimensionality sample-complexity separation and introduce a learning rule for modular tasks, targeting the scaling benefit that this paper suggests but cannot test in its infinite-data setup.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper offers a principled benchmark and metrics for diagnosing collapse and specialization across common modular MLP, attention, and recurrent architectures.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The known-rule generators, four-level routing ladder, five explicit utilization/specialization metrics, approximately 20,000-run factorial study, and 91 appendix figures form an unusually broad diagnostic package for 2022.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The benchmark and separation of collapse from specialization are useful, reusable contributions. The evidence strongly supports the narrow conclusion that a module split alone does not recover oracle specialization in these observed-context synthetic mixtures. It does not establish general real-world OOD or scaling benefits, and the paper overstates learned Modular superiority by not qualifying the decisive RNN-regression reversal. Later work supplies optimization methods, dynamics theory, finite-sample guarantees, and compositional or real-data tests.

reviewer_notes: Read all 46 extracted pages, including the model-class proof and every appendix performance, collapse, specialization, and OOD sweep. Rendered and inspected the aggregate performance/metric plots and representative MLP, MHA, and RNN ranking and curve panels; this revealed the RNN-regression contradiction hidden by the aggregate prose. Five direct competitors were checked against primary arXiv or OpenReview records on 2026-08-23. Findings labeled reviewer inference are not author claims.
